key_facts: **Port-wine stain** is a capillary **malformation**, present at birth, that grows with the child and never involutes.
Caused by a **somatic GNAQ** mutation; about 0.3% of newborns.
Darkens and thickens with age (cobblestoning, overgrowth).
Facial **V1** distribution: assess for **Sturge–Weber** (glaucoma, seizures); limb stain with overgrowth: consider Klippel–Trénaunay.
**Pulsed dye laser** (specialist) lightens it, best started early; camouflage for all.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: A **port-wine stain (PWS)** is a **capillary malformation**: present at birth as a flat red or purple patch, it **grows in proportion with the child**, may darken and thicken with age, and **never involutes**. It affects about **0.3%** of newborns.

sub: Equal sexes; any site, face commonest.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Dilated, malformed dermal capillaries, usually from a **somatic mosaic GNAQ** mutation; reduced nerve supply to the vessels lets them dilate progressively.

ul: **"It's a stork mark that will fade"**: salmon patches fade; port-wine stains do not.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: A port-wine stain is a patch of **malformed, progressively widening capillaries**.

mech.t: A GNAQ mutation in a developing cell gives a patch of abnormal vessels.
Dermal capillaries are dilated and increase in calibre with age.
mech.caption: Normal fine dermal capillaries (left) versus the widened, crowded capillaries of a port-wine stain (right).

mech.t: Poor sympathetic innervation of the vessels allows progressive dilation.
Over decades vessels enlarge further, causing darker colour, blebs and soft-tissue overgrowth.

histo: Dilated capillaries and venules in the papillary and reticular dermis without endothelial proliferation.

ul: Flat, well-demarcated pink, red or purple patch, often unilateral and following a dermatome-like segment.
With age: darker colour, thickening and **cobblestone** nodules (vascular blebs), soft-tissue overgrowth.
Blanches partly on pressure; does not grow out of proportion.

sub: V1 facial PWS with leptomeningeal angiomatosis and glaucoma: seizures, hemiparesis, learning difficulties.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical. MRI brain and eye review for facial V1 stains (Sturge–Weber); limb imaging and leg-length check for limb stains with overgrowth.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Pale pink, midline (nape, glabella, eyelids); fades in the first years
Absent or faint at birth, then rapid growth and involution

ul: Reassure for small, uncomplicated stains; camouflage cosmetics.
**Pulsed dye laser** is specialist, and earlier childhood referral is often preferred.
**Facial PWS in the V1 distribution: consider Sturge–Weber** (neurology and ophthalmology for glaucoma and seizures).
**Limb PWS with overgrowth: consider Klippel–Trénaunay** and related syndromes.

ladder.t: Pulsed dye laser via specialist; earlier childhood treatment often preferred.

refer.t: Facial V1 stain: ophthalmology (glaucoma) and neurology (Sturge–Weber).
Limb stain with overgrowth or asymmetry.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Facial segmental port-wine stain with eye or neurological symptoms (seizures, glaucoma).
Glaucoma, seizures (Sturge–Weber); limb overgrowth; bleeding from blebs; psychosocial impact.
Permanent; laser lightens but rarely clears.

pearls: A malformation is not a tumour: be clear with parents whether it is a PWS or a haemangioma.
PWS does not fade; salmon patches do.

quiz.a: No; it grows with the child and may darken and thicken.

quiz.q: Which syndrome must be considered with a V1 facial stain?
How is a salmon patch different?
quiz.a: Pale, midline and fades in early childhood.
